title: GS Caltex Wins Seventh Women's Volleyball Cup - 조선일보
content: Hur Sae-hong's cultural visit refocused team for record title victory [Sports Chosun Kim Young-rok Reporter] Seventh overall cup tournament victory. GS Caltex continues its winning momentum this year, following last year's dramatic championship final victory. GS Caltex claimed the title by defeating Korea Expressway Corporation with a set score of 3-2 in the women's final of the 2026 Yeosu·NH Nonghyup Cup Professional Volleyball Tournament held at Jinnam Gymnasium in Yeosu, South Jeolla Province, on October 18. This marked the club's seventh cup tournament victory in its history, achieved after a three-year gap, and set a new record for the most titles in the women's division. Behind this victory lay a special story. On October 13, after completing the first preliminary round match, the team visited GS Caltex Yeulmaru and Art Island Jangdo, representative cultural and artistic spaces in Yeosu, as part of a schedule arranged by club owner Hur Sae-hong. The visit aimed to refresh the team's atmosphere and provide relaxation after their first group-stage match. GS Caltex Yeulmaru, whose name combines the meanings of "cultural waves" and "traditional wooden floors," is a complex cultural and artistic space established and operated by GS Caltex in Yeosu as part of its social contribution initiatives. It offers high-quality performances and exhibitions to locals and visitors, featuring a grand theater, small theater, and exhibition halls designed by world-renowned architect Dominique Perrault. Alongside Art Island Jangdo, it has become a representative cultural and artistic space in Yeosu. The team toured major facilities, including the grand theater and rehearsal hall at GS Caltex Yeulmaru, and took commemorative photos on the outdoor terrace. They then moved to Art Island Jangdo, timed to coincide with the opening of the sea path. The team toured the island's exhibition hall, enjoyed a pianist's performance at a café on Jangdo, and used the time to relieve tension and communicate with teammates. This visit, arranged by club owner Hur Sae-hong to encourage the team, became a meaningful opportunity to refocus their minds ahead of the final. GS Caltex, energized by the visit to GS Caltex Yeulmaru, immediately turned the situation around. The team went on a three-game winning streak starting from the match following the visit and lifted the seventh cup tournament trophy by defeating Korea Expressway Corporation in the final. After the victory, club owner Hur Sae-hong sent a congratulatory message to the team: "A valuable victory, we are proud of you." He praised the team's performance, teamwork, and relentless focus until the end, which led to the seventh cup tournament title. He also expressed gratitude to GS Caltex Yeosu Plant employees who supported the team in Yeosu and encouraged the team to achieve good results in the 2026-2027 regular season. GS Caltex plans to build on the momentum from this 2026 Yeosu·NH Nonghyup Cup Professional Volleyball Tournament victory and accelerate preparations for the 2026-2027 season.

title: Lizzy G's Fine Gifts celebrates 15 years in Houston | Spring - Klein - Community Impact Newspaper

title: Intra-Company Housing Loans at Major Conglomerates Double - 조선일보
content: Outstanding balance reaches 637.07 billion won, up 92.8% from 2022 The scale of intra-company housing purchase loans from affiliates of South Korea’s seven major conglomerates has nearly doubled over three years. As rising home prices and tightened household loan regulations from financial institutions made it harder for employees to borrow from banks, demand has shifted to corporate-sponsored loans. According to data submitted by the Korea Fair Trade Commission to Song Eon-seog, a People Power Party lawmaker, on the 21st, the outstanding balance of intra-company housing purchase loans from affiliates of Hyundai Motor, SK, POSCO, Hanwha, Lotte, LG, and GS stood at 637.07 billion Korean won as of the end of August this year. This marks a 92.8% increase from the end of 2022 (330.47 billion Korean won). The outstanding balance has steadily risen: 438.65 billion Korean won in 2023, 578.29 billion Korean won in 2024, and 608.84 billion Korean won last year. By conglomerate, Hyundai Motor had the highest balance at 269.79 billion Korean won, followed by SK (179.8 billion Korean won), POSCO (84.75 billion Korean won), Hanwha (67.06 billion Korean won), Lotte (18.18 billion Korean won), LG (10.71 billion Korean won), and GS (6.78 billion Korean won). Notably, SK’s outstanding balance increased by 18.4% (27.98 billion Korean won) from 151.82 billion Korean won at the end of last year to 179.8 billion Korean won by the end of August this year. During the same period, POSCO rose by 14.1% (10.48 billion Korean won), GS by 8.8% (550 million Korean won), and Hanwha by 3.1% (1.99 billion Korean won). The advantage of intra-company loans lies in their low interest rates. By conglomerate, SK offers 0–3.0% annually, Hyundai Motor 1.0–2.7%, POSCO 1.5–2.0%, Hanwha 0–4.6%, GS 0–3.95%, Lotte 1.0–2.6%, and LG 0–2.0%. Some affiliates of SK, Hanwha, GS, and LG even provide housing purchase funds interest-free. However, Samsung and HD Hyundai were excluded from this survey. Samsung introduced an intra-company loan system on September 1 and was therefore not included in the survey, while HD Hyundai did not submit data without stating a reason. Song Eon-seog stated, “Intra-company loans should also be reflected in the Loan-to-Value ratio (LTV) and Debt Service Ratio (DSR) to apply the same lending principles to everyone.”

title: Pope Leo XIV: "The commitment to marriage and the family is more urgent than ever" – VIDEO - Rome Reports
content: Home - Pope - Pope Leo XIV: "The commitment to marriage and the family is more urgent than ever" – VIDEO Following his surgical operation, Pope Leo XIV presided over the general audience in St. Peter's Square, where he continued his commentary on the document Gaudium et Spes. On this occasion, he focused on conjugal love and the value of the family. Dear brothers and sisters, good morning and welcome! The first think I would like to say is thank you!. Thank you for the support of your prayers. Thanks be to God for His generosity. Let us all renew our trust in God’s goodness and mercy. The pastoral Constitution Gaudium et Spes(GS) of the Second Vatican Council, having illustrated in the first part the dignity of the person and his or her vocation in the world, goes on to consider, in the second part, “in the light of the Gospel and of human experience”, some of the most pressing contemporary issues (cf. GS, 46). It focuses primarily on marriage and the family, in the conviction that “the well-being of the individual and of human and Christian society is intimately linked with the healthy condition of that community produced by marriage and family” (GS, 47). To this end, it does not merely reaffirm their values and aims, but proposes a renewed conception of marriage as an “intimate partnership of married life and love” (GS, 48). By incorporating the legal dimension of marriage as a contract, the foundation of this union is recognized in the “conjugal covenant”, understood as the “human act whereby spouses mutually bestow and accept each another” (ibid.). The mutual self-giving of man and woman, such that ‘they are no longer two but one flesh’ (Mt 19:6), underlies the requirement for “total fidelity” and the “unbreakable oneness” of the spouses, finding vivid expression in the procreation and upbringing of children (cf. GS, 48). As a reflection of the Divine Trinity, conjugal and parental love, through the Sacrament of Marriage, is “governed and enriched by Christ’s redeeming power”, so that spouses may love one another “just as He loved the Church and handed Himself over on her behalf” (ibid.). Having shed light on the reality of marriage in the light of Christ’s love, which is the truth of both human and divine love, Gaudium et Spes turns its attention to conjugal love and marital fruitfulness. Not limited to erotic attraction, which it nonetheless encompasses, conjugal love involves the entire will of the spouses, enlivening the affections of their hearts and expressing itself through sentiments and gestures of tenderness (cf. GS, 49). Embracing the good of the whole person of both man and woman, who are equal in dignity, this love pervades the entire life of the spouses, finding expression in acts proper exclusively to marriage (cf. ibid.). Whilst signifying integral love from person to person, the unique intimacy between the spouses fosters their mutual self-giving and enriches their shared joy (cf. ibid.). Furthermore, the fruitfulness of conjugal love is expressed in the procreation of children, “the supreme gift of marriage” (GS, 50). By transmitting and educating human life, which must never be rejected, spouses become “cooperators with the love of God the Creator, and are, so to speak, the interpreters of that love” (ibid.). Called to this human and Christian responsibility, they are bound to allow themselves to be guided by a sound judgement regarding their own good and that of their children, whether already born or yet to be born. Such a judgement, which, in the final analysis, the spouses themselves must form before God, requires that their conscience conform to divine law, as interpreted by the Magisterium of the Church in the light of the Gospel (cf. ibid.). The emphasis on loving communion and procreative fruitfulness within marriage leads the Council to rule out the possibility of there being “a true contradiction … between the divine laws pertaining to the transmission of life, and those pertaining to authentic conjugal love” (GS, 51) and to affirm, instead, that “when there is question of harmonizing conjugal love with the responsible transmission of life”, one must “preserve the full sense of mutual self-giving and human procreation in the context of true love” (ibid.). From this it follows both that “from the moment of its conception life must be guarded with the greatest care”, renouncing “abortion and infanticide”; and that “the acts themselves which are proper to conjugal love and which are exercised in accord with genuine human dignity must be honoured with great reverence” (ibid.). The teaching of Gaudium et Spes on the conjugal and family community thus goes on to highlight the social function of the family, defined as “a school of deeper humanity” and “the foundation of society” (GS, 52), calling upon all those with social responsibilities, especially in the political and cultural spheres, to fulfil their duty to “work efficiently for the welfare of marriage and the family” (ibid.). Dear friends, this task is more urgent than ever before. The Church is well aware of this, as shown by the pastoral concern of the Popes who have succeeded one another since the last Council, right up to the two Synodal Assemblies convened by Pope Francis, which were addressed again in recent days by the Heads of the Eastern Catholic Churches and the Presidents of the Episcopal Conferences. May the Holy Family of Nazareth enlighten us on our journey and protect families throughout the world. I extend a warm welcome to all the English-speaking pilgrims and visitors taking part in today’s Audience. Upon all of you and your families, I invoke the joy and peace of our Lord Jesus Christ.  God bless you all! Dear brothers and sisters, in our ongoing catechesis on Gaudium et Spes, today we consider the dignity of marriage and the family in the context of contemporary challenges.  The Council Fathers recognized that the well-being of all in society is closely linked to the health of marriage and the family, and sought to present a renewed vision of conjugal love as an intimate partnership which reflects the life of the Trinity and is rooted in and enriched by the redemptive power of Christ.  Let us, therefore, pray for God’s blessing and protection upon all families.

title: Pope Leo XIV resumes general audiences after his operation: «Thank you for the support of your prayers - infovaticana
content:
by INFOVATICANA        |
October 21, 2026 Pope Leo XIV has resumed this Wednesday, October 21, the general audiences in St. Peter’s Square following the surgery he recently underwent. Before the faithful and pilgrims gathered in the Vatican, the Pontiff began his address with words of gratitude for the prayers received during his recovery: “The first thing I want to say to you is: thank you! Thank you for the support of your prayers. Thanks be to God for his generosity.” During the audience, Leo XIV continued his cycle of catechesis on the documents of the Second Vatican Council, dedicating his reflection to the teaching of the pastoral constitution Gaudium et spes on marriage and the family. The Pope recalled the importance of marital fidelity and indissolubility, the defense of life from conception, and society’s responsibility in protecting the family. Catechesis. The Documents of the Second Vatican Council. IV. Pastoral Constitution Gaudium et spes. 6. The Commitment to the Family in Today’s Society (GS, 47-52) Dear brothers and sisters, good morning and welcome! The first thing I want to say to you is: thank you! Thank you for the support of your prayers. Thanks be to God for his generosity. Let us all renew our trust in the goodness and mercy of God. The pastoral constitution Gaudium et spes (GS) of the Second Vatican Council, after having explained in its first part the dignity of the person and his or her vocation in the world, addresses in its second part, “in the light of the Gospel and of human experience,” some of the most urgent contemporary problems (cf. GS, 46). First of all, attention is focused on marriage and the family, with the conviction that “the well-being of the individual person and of both human and Christian society is closely bound up with the prosperity of the conjugal and family community” (GS, 47). To this end, the constitution does not merely reiterate the values and ends of marriage, but proposes a renewed understanding of it as an “intimate community of conjugal life and love” (GS, 48). Integrating the juridical dimension of marriage as a contract, it recognizes the foundation of this union in the “conjugal covenant,” understood as “the human act by which spouses give and receive each other mutually” (ibid.). The mutual self-giving of man and woman, “so that they are no longer two, but one flesh” (Mt 19:6), motivates the demand for “complete fidelity” and “indissoluble unity” of the spouses; and finds living expression in the procreation and education of children (cf. GS, 48). A reflection of the divine Trinity, conjugal and parental love, through the Sacrament of Marriage, “is ruled and enriched by the redemptive power of Christ,” so that spouses may love one another “as Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for her” (ibid.). Having illuminated the reality of marriage with the light of Christ’s love, which is the truth of both human and divine love, Gaudium et spes turns its attention to conjugal love and marital fruitfulness. Conjugal love is not limited to erotic attraction—which is also part of it—but encompasses the entire will of the spouses, rekindling their affection and expressing itself through sentiments and gestures of tenderness (cf. GS, 49). This love embraces the good of the whole person of man and woman, equal in dignity; it permeates the entire life of the spouses and finds expression in acts proper to marriage alone (cf. ibid.). The special intimacy of the spouses signifies the integral love of person to person, fosters mutual self-giving, and enriches their shared joy (cf. ibid.). The fruitfulness of conjugal love, moreover, is expressed in the procreation of children, “the most excellent gift of marriage” (GS, 50). By transmitting and educating human life, which must never be discarded, spouses become “cooperators in the love of God the Creator and, as it were, his interpreters” (ibid.). Called to this human and Christian responsibility, they must be guided by a right judgment concerning their own good and that of their children, already born or yet to come. This judgment, which ultimately the spouses must form personally before God, requires that their conscience be conformed to the divine law, interpreted by the Magisterium of the Church in the light of the Gospel (cf. ibid.). The appreciation of loving communion and procreative fruitfulness in marriage leads the Council to exclude the possibility of any “genuine contradiction between the divine laws of the transmission of life and the fostering of authentic conjugal love” (GS, 51); and to affirm, instead, that “when it is a question of harmonizing conjugal love with the responsible transmission of life, the moral character of any procedure does not depend solely on sincere intention or on an evaluation of motives. It must be determined by objective criteria, criteria drawn from the nature of the person and his acts, which preserve in the context of true love both the full sense of mutual self-giving and human procreation” (ibid.). It follows that “life must be safeguarded with the utmost care from the moment of conception,” rejecting “abortion and infanticide”; and that “the very acts proper to conjugal life, ordered according to genuine human dignity, must be respected with great reverence” (ibid.). The teaching of Gaudium et spes on the conjugal and family community thus underscores the social function of the family, which it defines as “the school of a richer humanity” and “the foundation of society” (GS, 52), reminding all those who bear social responsibilities, especially in the political and cultural spheres, of the duty to “contribute effectively to the advancement of marriage and the family” (ibid.). Dear friends, this commitment is more urgent than ever. The Church knows this well, as shown by the pastoral solicitude of the Popes who have succeeded one another since the last Council, up to the double Synodal Assembly desired by Pope Francis, on which the heads of the Eastern Catholic Churches and the presidents of the Episcopal Conferences have recently dialogued. May the Holy Family of Nazareth enlighten us on our journey and protect families throughout the world. I cordially greet the Spanish-speaking pilgrims. May the Holy Family of Nazareth protect all the families of the world. May God bless you. Thank you very much. Today we begin to reflect on the second part of the Pastoral Constitution Gaudium et spes, which deals with some of the most urgent problems of our time, including the family and marriage; the Council explains that marriage consists in a mutual self-giving that demands complete fidelity and an indissoluble unity. title: The Lexus V8 Sedan With A 7,300-RPM Redline That Never Got The M5's Respect - HotCars
content:
Angel Sergeev is a seasoned automotive journalist with over 15 years of experience covering the automotive industry. Born in Sofia, Bulgaria, he began his writing career in 2010 while pursuing a degree in Transportation Engineering.

His early work included contributions to the local edition of F1 Racing magazine (now GP Racing magazine) and roles at various automotive websites and magazines. In 2013, Angel joined Motor1.com (formerly WorldCarFans), where he dedicated over a decade to delivering daily news and feature articles. His expertise spans a wide range of topics, including electric vehicles, classic cars, and industry topics. Angel's commitment to automotive journalism is further demonstrated by his membership in the Bulgarian Car of the Year jury since 2013. There was a time when luxury sports sedans needed more than big horsepower figures to impress enthusiasts. Responsive engines, balanced handling, and engaging driving experiences mattered just as much. By the mid-2010s, however, the segment had become a horsepower arms race.     Turbochargers pushed outputs to new heights, while acceleration figures dominated the conversation. One Japanese automaker refused to follow the crowd, creating a V8-powered sedan that struggled for attention when new but now looks like something enthusiasts should have appreciated more. By 2016, the     BMW M5 had helped turn performance sedans into four-door supercars. The     F10 M5 packed a twin-turbocharged 4.4-liter V8 producing 560 horsepower, or 575 horsepower with the Competition Package. Mercedes-AMG's E63 S delivered 577 horsepower and 590 lb-ft of torque, while Audi's RS7 offered up to 605 horsepower in Performance trim. These machines combined luxury-car comfort with acceleration that could embarrass dedicated sports cars. Naturally, expectations changed. Reaching 60 mph in around four seconds was no longer remarkable, and some German rivals could comfortably beat that figure. Turbocharging delivered effortless acceleration, while ever-increasing horsepower figures dominated marketing campaigns. Unfortunately, that left little room for alternatives offering a different kind of excitement. A sedan with less than 500 horsepower suddenly seemed underpowered, even though that much muscle would have sounded outrageous a decade earlier. Against this backdrop, an unusual Japanese contender arrived with an engine that seemed to belong to another era. Rather than fitting turbochargers, its engineers chose a naturally aspirated 5.0-liter V8 producing 467 horsepower at 7,100 rpm and 389 lb-ft of torque at 4,800 rpm. Its 7,300-rpm redline revealed an engine designed to reward drivers who enjoyed exploring the upper end of the tachometer. The problem was that enthusiasm couldn't erase the horsepower deficit. Depending on the rival and version, the Japanese V8 trailed its turbocharged opponents by roughly 100 to 140 horsepower. Its eight-speed torque-converter automatic also lacked the immediate, mechanical feel of the M5's seven-speed dual-clutch transmission. Buyers comparing acceleration figures had plenty of reasons to favor Germany. That unusual contender was the 2016–2020     Lexus GS F, the Japanese automaker's answer to the BMW M5 and Mercedes-AMG E63. Its centerpiece was the Yamaha-assisted 2UR-GSE naturally aspirated V8, an engine with roots in the earlier IS F. Instead of chasing horsepower records,     Lexus focused on throttle response and high-rpm performance. The engine featured both direct and port fuel injection, along with variable valve timing that allowed it to operate using the fuel-saving Atkinson cycle under lighter loads. Under hard acceleration, it switched to the conventional Otto cycle for maximum power. The GS F wasn't slow, either. Official data showed a 4.4-second sprint to 60 mph and a 12.9-second quarter-mile at 113 mph, while Lexus also quoted an electronically limited top speed of 168 mph. Its 467 horsepower went exclusively to the rear wheels through an eight-speed automatic. However, its character mattered more than the numbers. While turbocharged German rivals delivered enormous torque low in the rev range, the     Lexus built excitement as engine speed increased. An M5 could surge forward without needing a downshift, while the GS F encouraged drivers to select a lower gear and chase its 7,300-rpm redline. The brand also knew that making a sedan weighing more than 4,000 pounds feel agile required clever engineering. Its standard Torque Vectoring Differential distributed power between the rear wheels to improve cornering behavior. Drivers could choose Standard for balanced responses, Slalom for sharper turning, or Track for greater stability. The GS F also received reinforced body components, tuned suspension, and large Brembo brakes. Interestingly, Lexus initially skipped adjustable dampers, relying on a carefully tuned fixed setup. Period testing measured 0.93 g of cornering grip from its 4,128-pound test car, matching the M5's figure. Time has made the GS F's original disadvantages more appealing. Its naturally aspirated V8, rear-wheel-drive layout, and focus on driver involvement recall qualities that made the     E39 BMW M5 an enthusiast favorite. That earlier     BMW used a naturally aspirated 4.9-liter V8 producing 394 horsepower in U.S. specification, paired with a six-speed manual. The Lexus couldn't recreate that manual-shifting experience, but both rewarded drivers who appreciated linear throttle response and engines that loved to rev. Ironically, the GS F couldn't match the F10 M5's acceleration, yet it preserved some of the characteristics that made earlier M5s so desirable. Long-term dependability strengthens its appeal. The 2UR-GSE has earned a reputation for durability, while its naturally aspirated design avoids the turbochargers and associated hardware found in more complex rivals. That doesn't make it maintenance-free—owners have reported coolant leaks around the engine's valley plate, while aging water pumps and expensive performance brakes deserve attention. Still, owning a high-revving V8 without worrying about two turbochargers has obvious advantages. The GS F also retained Lexus's trademark refinement, making it a comfortable daily driver. Lexus initially hoped to sell around 2,000 examples annually in the United States, but the broader GS lineup struggled as buyers increasingly favored SUVs. By 2019, the entire GS range accounted for just 4% of Lexus passenger-car sales, totaling 3,378 vehicles, and held less than 1% of the midsize luxury sedan market. Those figures included every GS variant, but they showed how weak demand had become. Lexus discontinued the lineup after the 2020 model year. Today, the GS F looks like a potential future classic. Its understated styling helped it fly under the radar, with quad exhaust outlets, an aggressive grille, and a subtle rear spoiler hinting at its performance. Beneath that discreet exterior sat a V8 that could scream to 7,300 rpm, a rear-wheel-drive chassis with clever torque management, and enough comfort for long journeys. We want to hear from you. title: In-House Housing Loans from Major Groups Nearly Double Over Three Years - 조선일보
content: In-house loans surge 92.8% as employees seek alternatives amid rising prices, tighter bank rules The scale of in-house housing purchase loans from affiliates of seven major domestic groups has nearly doubled over three years. As housing prices rise and financial institutions tighten household loan regulations, making it difficult to borrow from banks, demand has surged for in-house loans provided by companies to their employees. According to data submitted by the Korea Fair Trade Commission to Song Eon-seog, a People Power Party lawmaker, on the 21st, the outstanding balance of in-house housing purchase loans from affiliates of seven groups—Hyundai Motor Company, SK, POSCO, Hanwha, Lotte, LG, and GS—stood at 637.07 billion Korean won as of the end of August this year. This represents a 92.8% increase from the end of 2022 (330.47 billion Korean won). The outstanding balance of in-house loans steadily increased to 438.65 billion Korean won in 2023, 578.29 billion Korean won in 2024, and 608.84 billion Korean won last year. By group, Hyundai Motor Company had the highest outstanding balance at 269.79 billion Korean won, followed by SK (179.8 billion Korean won), POSCO (84.75 billion Korean won), Hanwha (67.06 billion Korean won), Lotte (18.18 billion Korean won), LG (10.71 billion Korean won), and GS (6.78 billion Korean won). Notably, SK’s in-house loan balance increased by 18.4% (27.98 billion Korean won) to 179.8 billion Korean won as of the end of August this year, up from 151.82 billion Korean won at the end of last year. During the same period, POSCO saw a 14.1% increase (10.48 billion Korean won), GS rose by 8.8% (550 million Korean won), and Hanwha increased by 3.1% (1.99 billion Korean won). The advantage of in-house loans is their low interest rates. By group, the loan interest rates are as follows: SK 0–3.0% annually, Hyundai Motor Company 1.0–2.7%, POSCO 1.5–2.0%, Hanwha 0–4.6%, GS 0–3.95%, Lotte 1.0–2.6%, and LG 0–2.0%. Some affiliates of SK, Hanwha, GS, and LG even offer interest-free loans for housing purchases. However, Samsung and HD Hyundai were excluded from this survey. Samsung was not included as it newly introduced an in-house loan system on September 1, while HD Hyundai did not submit data without providing a specific reason. Song Eon-seog stated, “In-house loans should also be reflected in the loan-to-value (LTV) ratio and debt service ratio (DSR) to apply the same lending principles to everyone.”

title: GS Caltex Secures Seventh Cup Title with Owner's Support - 조선일보
content: Chairman Hur's Cultural Visit Rejuvenated Team, Securing Historic Seventh Title [OSEN=Lee Hoo-kwang Reporter] Behind GS Caltex's seventh overall victory in the Cup Tournament was the owner's generous support and encouragement. GS Caltex defeated Korea Expressway Corporation with a set score of 3-2 in the women's final of the 2026 Yeosu·NH Nonghyup Cup Professional Volleyball Tournament held at the Yeosu Jinnam Gymnasium on October 18, securing the championship. This victory marked GS Caltex's return to the Cup Tournament summit after three years, recording their seventh overall Cup Tournament title—the most in women's division history. A special story lay behind this triumph. On the 20th, GS Caltex shared, "After completing the first preliminary round on October 13, the team visited 'GS Caltex Yeulmaru' and 'Jangdo, the Art Island,' representative cultural and artistic spaces in Yeosu, as arranged by Chairman Hur Sae-hong, to rest and rejuvenate." Regarding this visit, GS Caltex explained, "It was organized at the invitation of Chairman Hur Sae-hong to shift the team's mood and refresh them after their first group-stage match. GS Caltex Yeulmaru, which embodies the meanings of 'cultural waves' and 'traditional wooden floors,' is a complex cultural and artistic space established and operated in Yeosu as part of GS Caltex's social contribution initiatives. It offers high-quality performances and exhibitions to locals and visitors, featuring a grand theater, small theater, and exhibition halls designed by world-renowned architect Dominique Perrault. Alongside Jangdo, the Art Island, it has become a representative cultural and artistic space in Yeosu." The team toured major facilities, including the grand theater and rehearsal hall at GS Caltex Yeulmaru, and took commemorative photos on the outdoor terrace. They then moved to Jangdo, the Art Island, timed with the opening of the sea path. The team observed the exhibition hall on Jangdo and listened to a pianist's performance at a café on the island, easing tensions accumulated during the tournament and communicating with teammates. GS Caltex emphasized, "This visit, initiated by Chairman Hur Sae-hong's encouragement, became a meaningful time for the team to regroup mentally ahead of the final." Inspired by the visit to GS Caltex Yeulmaru and rejuvenated, GS Caltex immediately turned the tide. The team went on a three-game winning streak from the subsequent matches, defeating Korea Expressway Corporation in the final to lift the Cup Tournament trophy for the seventh time. After the victory, Chairman Hur Sae-hong sent a congratulatory message to the team: "A valuable victory, we are proud of you." He praised the team's performance, teamwork, and relentless focus until the end, encouraging them. He also expressed gratitude to GS Caltex Yeosu Plant employees who supported the team in Yeosu and wished the team success in the 2026-2027 regular season. GS Caltex added, "We plan to build momentum from this 2026 Yeosu·NH Nonghyup Cup Professional Volleyball Tournament victory and accelerate preparations for the 2026-2027 season."

title: Colombian Star Karol G’s ‘BbY WOW’ Outlasts Taylor Swift for Sixth Week Atop Global 200 - Martin Cid Magazine
content: Karol G’s “BbY WOW” is back on top of Billboard’s global charts, and the most telling part of its run is what it had to beat to stay there. For one week, Taylor Swift’s “Patient Zero” took the crown with exactly the kind of launch the modern music business is built to produce. The following week, the song Karol G made with Spanish artists Judeline and rusowsky took it back, and it has held on since. That is an odd career for a track nobody planned as the biggest hit of her life. “BbY WOW” started as a Karol G solo song and became a trio late, when she reopened it to two artists from Spain’s alternative scene. Its climb was already underway before the dance trend that much of the coverage credits for its rise. Up close, the streaming giant of the autumn looks less like a campaign and more like a last-minute creative call that paid off. Billboard’s own numbers make the contrast plain. “Patient Zero,” one of four new songs on Swift’s deluxe edition The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, opened at No. 1 on the Billboard Global 200 and Global Excl. U.S. charts dated Oct. 10 with 70.7 million streams and 80,000 copies sold worldwide, according to Luminate. “BbY WOW” slipped to No. 3 that week after four weeks on top. Seven days later it was No. 1 again with 46.2 million streams while “Patient Zero” fell to No. 2, and on the charts dated Oct. 24 Swift’s single sits at No. 3. The new tracking week, Oct. 9 to 15, gave “BbY WOW” 45.4 million streams worldwide, down just 2% from the week before, plus 1,000 copies sold. About three of every four of those streams, 34.1 million, came from outside the United States. Shakira and Burna Boy’s World Cup anthem “Dai Dai” owned the summer before “BbY WOW” ended its reign in September; Billboard noted at the time that Karol G’s song was the first No. 1 on the global charts performed mostly in Spanish since Bad Bunny’s “DtMF” finished its run in March. For Karol G, it is new territory. Her only previous leader on the lists, “TQG” with Shakira, topped them for its debut week in March 2023. “BbY WOW” gave her a first multi-week global No. 1 in September and, in the U.S., her second Hot 100 top 10 after that same Shakira duet. How the song reached its final shape is the part the chart celebrations skip. Judeline told NYLON that she wrote with Karol G in Malibu, with Tainy and rusowsky in the room, while the Colombian star was rehearsing for Coachella, and that “BbY WOW” “was supposed to be a song for her and only her.” About two weeks before the album came out, Karol called asking for Judeline and rusowsky on it. “We did the song in two days,” Judeline said. She cut her verse in a studio she tracked down near her hometown, hidden behind what looked from the street like a fried-fish shop, and the song was out a week later. Karol G described the same decision to Rolling Stone, as quoted by Songfacts: “The first version was just me. But I felt like, live, I wanted to sing that song with more people on stage and for it to turn into a party.” The credits carry that collaborative streak. Karol, Tainy, Omer Fedi, Judeline and rusowsky all share production, over a flip of the Coolie Dance Riddim that Nina Sky’s “Move Ya Body” made famous in 2004. Judeline’s hand on the album goes well beyond the feature: she co-wrote four songs on No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, including the opener “Te Llevas To.” In France, NRJ framed the run as the work of a TikTok choreography by the creator trio Los Menor3s, posted on Aug. 24, whom Karol later brought on stage during her U.S. tour. The trend was real and it spread fast. The chart timeline, though, says it poured fuel on a fire that was already lit. The song entered Spotify’s global daily chart on Aug. 12, according to La República, and jumped from No. 171 to No. 37 on the Global 200 in the tracking week that closed on Aug. 20, Complex reported, four days before the dance went up. The weeks that followed, a 37-to-5 leap on a 45% gain in streams and then the move to No. 1, are where the song and the trend pushed together. There is a fair caveat inside all of this. Billboard’s global charts blend official streams and download sales from more than 200 territories, and in practice they are streaming rankings: “BbY WOW” sells around 1,000 copies a week worldwide. “Biggest song in the world” now means the song most replayed on platforms where playlists and short-video trends do much of the distribution. That system rewards a huge opening, as Swift’s week showed. It also rewards the songs listeners keep returning to, which is how a track that sold a fraction of her copies took the top spot back. For the two Spaniards, the scale has changed completely. Judeline, who grew up in Cádiz, became the first Spanish woman to reach No. 1 on Spotify’s global chart, according to LatiNation and N+. In 2024 she played London’s The Lower Third to 250 people; on Sept. 5 she closed her first headlining tour in front of 26,500 at Plaza Mayor in Valladolid, she told NYLON. rusowsky, the Madrid producer and singer born Ruslán Mediavilla and known for his bedroom-pop records, scored his first Hot 100 top 10 alongside her. No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, Karol G’s sixth studio album, came out Aug. 7 and debuted at No. 1 on Top Latin Albums. Her tour is still working through the Americas and reaches Europe next year, opening in Barcelona on June 3, 2027, with Paris on July 1. The song Karol G first recorded alone has already spent six times as many weeks at No. 1 on Billboard’s global chart as the rest of her catalog combined. title: Lonza and Onava collaborate to accelerate AI-native biologics discovery with GS Ori-Go Vectors - Manufacturing Chemist
content: Lonza, the world's leading contract development and manufacturing organisation (CDMO), and Onava, a biotechnology company building an AI-native platform for biologics discovery, announced today a collaboration to support AI-enabled drug discovery through experimental validation using Lonza’s GS Gene Expression System platform with GS Ori-Go vectors Under the Research Evaluation Agreement (REA), Onava will leverage Lonza’s GS Gene Expression System technology through Lonza’s flexible evaluation framework. The agreement enables Onava to connect computational prediction with biological data generation earlier and at greater scale in discovery. Data generated using the GS Gene Expression System platform will be incorporated into subsequent design cycles, creating a closed-loop system that helps refine Onava’s predictive models, supports earlier candidate assessment and improve development readiness. Peter Droc, Vice President, Head of Licensing, Lonza, commented: AI-enabled drug discovery depends on the ability to connect computational design with robust experimental validation. By providing access to the GS Gene Expression System platform with GS Ori-Go vectors through a flexible Research Evaluation Agreement, we can help customers generate high-quality biological data earlier in discovery, refine candidates with greater confidence and make better-informed development decisions. We are pleased to support Onava as it applies AI-enabled approaches to advance the next generation of therapeutics. The collaboration is expected to extend beyond a single program, with Onava planning to use GS Gene Expression System technology across multiple external partnerships as well as selected internal programs. As candidates advance, Lonza is well positioned to support continued development through its integrated cell line development, process development and manufacturing capabilities. For AI-native biologics discovery, expression is not simply a downstream manufacturing consideration; it is a critical source of training data. By incorporating Lonza’s GS Gene Expression System and GS Ori-Go vectors into our platform, we can generate consistent, experimentally grounded data across large numbers of AI-designed molecules and feed it directly back into our models. This improves our ability to design not only for biological function, but for the developability and manufacturability that therapeutics require. By combining AI-enabled discovery, proven expression technologies and a flexible licensing framework, Lonza and Onava aim to help translate computational insights into development-ready therapeutic candidates more efficiently.

title: 310-HP V6, AWD, Torque Vectoring - Buick's Final Sports Sedan Costs Half As Much As A New Golf R - CarBuzz
content: If there's one thing that we gearheads can agree on, it's that new car prices are ridiculous. In fact, the average price for a new car in the US has hit $50,000. That's almost exactly the price of a new  Volkswagen Golf R, and while it may be fast, safe, and comfortable, what if your money were best spent on something used? Something a bit more practical with similar performance, perhaps? Enter: the Buick Regal GS. This American sports sedan was more than a rebadged European family car, offering performance and space without the high price tag. You can now easily find this car for less than half the price of a used Golf R – something we still can't quite understand. Here's why... Buick knew that time was running out for its sedans in the 2010s. The automaker's SUV sales were surging, and while the fifth-gen Regal sedan was a great car, its looks were becoming outdated and customers started looking elsewhere. That's why in 2017, the sixth-generation Regal debuted with a much more handsome exterior and interior. The writing was on the wall for this car, which is why Buick decided to go out with a bang. The GS trim was introduced as the halo version, featuring a larger 3.6L V6 engine and sportier cosmetics. While we think of ultra-exclusive Italian supercars as collectibles, the Regal GS's low production number of around 1,300 means it's exclusive and represents perhaps the last true performance-oriented Buick like this. For the company that gave us the GNX and Skylark GS, it's safe to say that collectors love the last-of-the-line model.But nostalgia alone doesn't justify a purchase – so what does the GS actually deliver behind the wheel? The GS badge meant the Regal was ready to be driven hard. Its 3.6L V6 engine has strong links to the Chevrolet Colorado and GMC Canyon of the same vintage, but here it makes 310 horsepower and 282 lb-ft through a clever all-wheel-drive system. That AWD system isn't old-fashioned, either, as it has torque vectoring capabilities that mean it can send up to 100% of the engine's power to an individual rear wheel through two computer-controlled clutches. This AWD system is also used in the TourX wagon, but in the GS driving mode, it will send more of its power to the rear wheels. This driving mode also firms up the adaptive suspension, quickens throttle response, makes the steering heavier, and lets the nine-speed automatic hold onto gears longer. It's exactly what you want in a sports sedan – the ability to be comfortable in most situations and then turn into a sports car when asked. Beyond the engine and AWD system, there's a lot to love. The transmission is smooth, it can reach 60 miles per hour in under six seconds, and reaches a top speed of 167 miles per hour. The GS' Brembo brakes are also solid. Without turbochargers, the V6 produces linear power that you'll want to unleash. It makes peak torque at 5,200 rpm and peak power at 6,800 rpm, meaning it has that old-school rev-happy character. So, it's half the price of a new Golf R – is it half the amount of fun? Definitely not. The V6 in the GS makes only 18 hp and 13 lb-ft of torque less than Volkswagen's 2.0L turbo-four, and while it may be a second slower to 60 miles per hour, it offers much of the same on-paper performance. Of course, the Golf R's 4Motion all-wheel-drive system is much more modern and advanced, leading to super-grippy all-weather performance, but the Buick isn't far behind. The Regal's performance means it's easily faster than the Golf GTI, and while the modern hot hatches may be more agile, the Buick's slightly longer wheelbase may make it more stable at speed. Volkswagen offers the Golf R with standard adaptive suspension, meaning just like the Regal, it's a superb daily driver but turns into a monster when asked. The best thing about both the Regal GS and the Golf R is how they combine performance and everyday usability. This stretches to the design, as the GS badges on the Buick are subdued and, unless you were looking, you wouldn't be able to tell it's the flagship. The Golf looks a bit racier with its spoiler and vents, especially in a bright color that complements its stance. We love the design of both, but those wanting a sleeper will prefer the GS. Even with the younger Golf in comparison, the Buick Regal GS isn't as sparse as you may think. There's ventilated seating, keyless start, and most impressively, massage controls for both front seats. Of course, the Golf has the larger infotainment display, as that's where the industry is heading, but the GS has smartphone connectivity so you're not stuck with an outdated system. The only thing that we can see the Golf having over the Regal is rear heated seats and a better sound system. It's worth mentioning size, too, as the Buick wins easily here. The Golf manages just under 20 cubic feet of space in the cargo bay, while the GS can manage 31.5 cubes. It also has more rear legroom at 36.9 inches compared to 35 inches, and its hatchback design makes it highly practical. With only 1,300 units made, the Buick Regal GS isn't super common on the marketplace, so when one pops up, we'd certainly be reaching out quickly. You won't have to worry about high-mileage examples, either, as the LGX family of 3.6L V6 engines is said to be reliable when properly maintained. It's an improvement over previous GM blocks like this. Very high-mileage examples may benefit from a cleanup around the intake valves, which can clog with carbon buildup. Some owners also recommend getting the timing chain checked out, so a recent service stamp for this is ideal. Given its status as a sports sedan, make sure you're getting a well-cared-for example with service history. At the time of writing, we can see listings range from $20–$25k for cars with around 60,000 miles. You can dip under $20k if you go for listings with around 100,000 miles, and we wouldn't be worried about reliability with its decent record. Even if you find an unreliable example, you'll still be way under the Golf R's price with some repairs and servicing. Can you feel the 18 hp difference between these two cars by the seat of your pants? Probably not. The Regal GS is a more practical sleeper sedan that has just as many creature comforts as the Golf, without the intrusive new-car chimes and alerts. And for half the price, you can't go wrong. title: The Adventure Bike That Makes 600-Mile Weekends Look Casual - Top Speed
content: The United States has over four million miles of public roads, a massive network where heavy highway cruisers and full-dress tourers rule. Over the past two decades, though, full-size adventure bikes have quietly been making inroads as the ultimate long-distance machines. Showroom ads love to push desert-racing fantasies and spec-sheet bragging rights, but anyone who actually tours knows the truth. Big days come down to simple things: wind protection, stability, and not feeling completely beaten up after eight hours in the saddle. In this crowded class, one machine stands out by turning exhausting cross-country trips into easy, casual weekend rides. The trouble with touring America is that smooth asphalt only covers part of the map. Huge stretches of the country — national forest roads, public lands, cracked mountain passes, and rough county routes — rarely get fresh pavement. When the road turns to potholes or washboard, an 800-pound road tourer hits a hard wall. On the other hand, lightweight dual-sport motorcycles can handle the dirt, but their buzzy single-cylinder engines and tiny windshields make high-speed interstate riding miserable. You either give up highway comfort, or you miss out on the most beautiful, remote roads in the country. BMW figured out this dual-purpose formula back in 1980 with the original R 80 G/S. Proven by winning the grueling Paris-Dakar rally and improved over four decades, BMW showed that an opposed boxer-twin engine was built for long-haul durability. The brand eventually turned this setup into the gold standard for all-road travel. The R 1300 GS Adventure has a very reasonable base price of $23,795, but BMW's infamous packaging system for options means that should you want to add certain things to it, it can climb in a hurry. For example, if you want to add the automatic gearbox option as a standalone unit, it is under $1,000, but it is available only as part of a package. Therefore, the minimum price you have to pay for a GSA with the automated system is $28,235. It is safe to assume that you will end up spending around $30,000 on one, which is the price for German engineering mastery. BMW has gradually been updating its engines, and the R 1300 GS gets one of the biggest updates in the form of an optional automatic gearbox. Another first is that the variable valve timing adjusts not just timing but lift as well, all of which combines to offer bulletproof engineering with long-distance comfort. To run quickly through the specs, it displaces 1,300 cc from its boxer-twin engine. It has variable valve timing on the intake valves called BMW ShiftCam, a short-stroke design, four valves per head, and a relatively high compression ratio of 13.3:1. It generates 145 horsepower at 7,750 RPM and 110 pound-feet of torque at 6,500 RPM. In standard form, it is mated to a six-speed manual gearbox with an assist-and-slipper clutch. A two-way quickshifter is an optional extra, as is the automated manual gearbox. The ASA automatic performs exactly like a fully automatic gearbox — you need to operate only the throttle and brakes, and you can switch it off and use it as a full manual gearbox if you prefer to have full control yourself. As with all halo GS models, it uses a driveshaft to transmit power to the wheel. Reliability is crucial for an engine that wants to rack up 600 miles every weekend, and the R 1300 GS Adventure nails that, too. And there are a few reasons for this. BMW has been making boxer engines since 1923, and over the century the company has perfected the formula. It’s the most advanced boxer engine BMW has ever created, and a lot of focus has gone into making it dependable. Additionally, the boxer engine used here is relatively low-stress and low-revving, which adds to its reliability. And the opposed cylinders result in inherent primary balance, reducing vibration and wear on mechanical parts. Meanwhile, the protruding cylinder heads and carbon shaft drive make routine maintenance very easy. It’s still not perfect, though. More tech means there are more things to go wrong. Plus, some major service jobs, like changing the clutch plates, require taking off the subframe. And there was also a fire recall back in 2024 due to a faulty starter. But as far as luxury adventure tourers go, the BMW R 1300 GS Adventure remains one of the safest non-Japanese bets today. The R 1300 GS frame has also been updated, and it is now a two-piece chassis that resembles a diamond frame and uses the engine as a stressed member. The subframe is bolted on, and the result is a 26.5-pound decrease in overall weight compared to its predecessor. It uses BMW's proprietary Paralever and Telelever suspension setup; there is a wishbone front suspension with a central shock and a single-sided swingarm that also houses the driveshaft. It offers 8.3 inches of travel at the front and 8.7 inches at the rear, which is significantly more than its non-Adventure sibling. The brakes are up to the task of hauling this big ADV’s mass down to a halt quickly, with twin 310 mm front discs with radial four-piston fixed calipers and a 285 mm rear disc with a two-piston floating caliper. It uses a 19-inch front wheel and a 17-inch rear wheel; alloy rims are standard, but upgrades are available. It is a similar story with the tires — tubeless radials are standard, but you can choose more aggressive, dirt-focused ones from the options list. In standard form, despite its height, it feels effortless at highway speeds. The R 1300 GS Adventure weighs almost 600 pounds unladen with a full fuel tank. That 593-pound figure is actually par for the course for the segment when a massive fuel tank is involved, but in the case of the BMW, the weight is carried down low because the cylinders are horizontal, and therefore it feels very well-balanced and easy at parking-lot speeds. BMW has also redesigned the huge 7.9-gallon tank to hold the fuel as low as possible, which also helps. This is the ADV with the longest range today. This is a large motorcycle that is 89.8 inches long and 39.8 inches wide, with a 34.6-inch seat height. A 60.4-inch wheelbase gives it great stability not just on the highway, but also while hooning around in the dirt. It starts with a 6.5-inch TFT screen that has Bluetooth connectivity and navigation as standard features. The electronics package is well-rounded as well, thanks to the by-wire throttle and six-axis IMU. Going into the standard details will be an exercise in repeating ourselves, so what we will do instead is look at the upgrades. The suspension has standard DSA, which translated into layman's terms is electronic suspension adjustability. This has automatic damping and spring rate control, and the rear preload can also be set. The options list is comprehensive, but it is also dependent on packages; you cannot always include individual items. As a flagship vehicle from a premium brand, the R 1300 GS Adventure has an extremely impressive feature set, as befits the ultimate adventure motorcycle. We want to hear from you. title: GS Global invests in carbon credit firm to expand trading business - The Korea Times
content: GS Global CEO Kim Sung-won, center, poses with Hooxi Partners Co-CEO Lee Haeng-youl, left, and Hooxi Partners Co-CEO Cho Seong-hoon after signing a strategic investment agreement in Seoul, Monday. Courtesy of GS Global GS Global is expanding into carbon credit trading through an equity investment in Hooxi Partners, a Korean carbon credit specialist, seeking to monetize emissions reductions from its existing eco-friendly businesses. GS Global said Tuesday that the investment would establish a strategic partnership, combining Hooxi Partners’ carbon reduction expertise with GS Global’s global network and trading capabilities. The investment comes as Korea's fourth emissions trading scheme, covering 2026-2030, takes effect. Tighter emissions caps, expanded paid allocations and stricter global carbon regulations are raising the cost of securing carbon credits and increasing exposure to price volatility. GS Global aims to turn carbon credits into a new growth engine. Founded in 2021, Hooxi Partners offers services ranging from carbon credit methodology development and emissions reduction project management to securing Korean Offset Credits (KOCs) and forward trading. The company focuses on transportation-related emissions reduction projects, particularly the transition to electric vehicles. It also operates emissions management platforms and provides corporate consulting. Its program-based emissions reduction model groups multiple individual projects under a single registration and management framework, reducing administrative and verification burdens while enabling emissions reductions on a larger scale. Hooxi Partners' revenue surged to 3.2 billion won ($2.4 million) in 2025 from 200 million won in 2024 and is projected to reach 7.8 billion won this year. The company turned profitable in 2025 and is expected to generate a net profit of around 3.3 billion won in 2026. GS Global plans to integrate the partnership with its existing businesses, including electric bus adoption, solar and other renewable energy projects, biomass and resource recycling. It aims to convert emissions reductions from these activities into Korean Offset Credits (KOCs) and supply them to domestic and overseas buyers. The company also plans to draw on its overseas customer network in steel, energy and industrial materials, along with Hooxi Partners' expertise, to identify and develop carbon reduction projects in international markets. "Through this investment, we aim to enter the growing carbon credit market early and establish a new growth area," a GS Global official said, adding that the company would continue to expand cooperation on carbon reduction projects at home and abroad. title: OPM Finalizes Rule Eliminating Time-in-Grade For GS Promotions - FedSmith.com
content: OPM has ended the 52-week time-in-grade wait for GS promotions. Here is what changes and what does not. The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has finalized a rule eliminating the governmentwide time-in-grade requirement, a restriction that generally made General Schedule (GS) employees wait 52 weeks at a lower grade before they could be considered for promotion. The change takes effect January 19, 2027. The final rule adopts OPM’s May proposed rule substantially unchanged. However, the details show that the end of time-in-grade will not automatically mean faster promotions. The restriction applied to competitive service GS positions at GS-6 and above. A candidate generally needed 52 weeks in a position one grade lower than the job being filled or two grades lower for certain positions in occupations that advance in two-grade steps. It did not apply to Federal Wage System employees, pay-banded positions, most excepted service employees or applicants hired through open competitive examination. The requirement dates to the Whitten Amendment of the early 1950s and survived as a regulation after the underlying statutory requirement ended in 1978. OPM Director Scott Kupor said in a statement, “The old rule made the calendar a gatekeeper. If someone is qualified and ready to take on more responsibility, the government shouldn’t make them wait another year just because the clock says so.” For many employees, perhaps not right away. OPM noted in the rule that its governmentwide qualification standards have historically included a comparable one-year service period. In OPM’s words, time-in-grade “largely duplicated” a requirement imposed elsewhere. OPM says it is separately reviewing that requirement, including whether qualification should be measured by elapsed time at all. Until that review produces changes, an employee moving up a standard career ladder may find the practical timeline looks much the same. OPM cited comments from employees who said time-in-grade held them back despite relevant experience, including: Yes. Agencies may set their own job-related prerequisites, including a minimum period in grade, through their written merit promotion plans, provided the requirements are applied consistently. OPM also confirmed that eliminating time-in-grade does not require agencies to accelerate career ladder promotions. OPM set the effective date 90 days out to give agencies time to update their merit promotion plans, which may involve bargaining with unions. Until an agency revises its plan, the existing plan remains in effect minus the time-in-grade restriction. The rule also drops the requirement for OPM approval of training agreements that allowed accelerated promotions, along with the limit of two promotions in 52 weeks under those agreements. OPM tied the change directly to its new performance appraisal rule finalized in July, which allows a standardized, or forced, distribution of performance ratings. OPM said limiting top ratings will make them a more meaningful signal of which employees are ready for higher-graded work. However, OPM stated that a rating of record is neither required nor sufficient for promotion. Agencies may also weigh demonstrated results, technical assessments, structured interviews and assessments of an employee’s potential. OPM said removing the waiting period supports its effort to make federal service more competitive for early-career talent, which it is also pursuing through its Early Careers Initiative and U.S. Tech Force. In a blog post, Kupor wrote that only about 7% of the federal workforce is early career, compared with roughly 22% to 23% of the broader American workforce. This is not OPM’s first attempt. The agency proposed eliminating time-in-grade in 1994, 1995 and 2008, and finalized a rule in late 2008 before withdrawing it in 2009 pending a broader review that was never completed. OPM received 75 comments, most of them supportive. A minority argued the 52-week wait served as an objective check against managers fast-tracking favored employees. OPM responded that time-in-grade never measured whether a candidate was qualified and that merit promotion rules, which require job-related criteria and documentation, still govern selections. It declined requests for mandatory review boards, public reporting and a delayed effective date. The most immediate effect is likely to fall on employees with outside or nontraditional experience, and on agencies that want to move them up faster. title: Electrifying Alpine ski season set to start in style following sensational announcements - International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS)
content: Mikaela Shiffrin (USA/Atomic) swerving some Slaloms, Lucas Pinheiro Braathen (BRA/Atomic) targeting the Super G and Lara Gut-Behrami (SUI) cheering on from the sidelines as 22-year-old Emma Aicher (GER/Head) looks to take over; welcome to the exciting new world of the 2027 Audi FIS Alpine Ski World Cup season. It has been a wildly eventful seven months since the planet’s finest last took to the slopes. Here is everything you need to know as we count down until the curtain raiser in Sölden, Austria this weekend, 24-25 October, with the FIS Alpine Skiing World Championships shining like a jewel in February 2027. From the moment she made her maiden tour appearance as a 15-year-old in Spindleruv Mlyn in 2011, Shiffrin has hogged the headlines. But now the most successful World Cup skier of all time has grabbed centre stage not for what she is doing on the slopes, but for decisions she has taken off them. For the first time since that teenage debut, Shiffrin will rarely be seen on Slalom skis this season. Instead, the woman who secured a record-extending ninth World Cup Slalom Globe in March will place her primary focus on the Giant Slalom and the Super G, two disciplines in which she has long been short of her best. It is an electrifying development that throws up an almost endless list of fascinating questions. Just two years after suffering PTSD following a heavy crash in Killington, can Shiffrin rediscover the form that made her the most successful women’s World Cup GS skier to date? Can she find the speed to challenge in the Super G, a discipline in which she has not won since December 2022? Who will step into Shiffrin’s place in the Slalom? What does all this mean for the Overall Globe? Fans will get their first answers when the American superstar takes on Sölden’s famous Rettenbach Glacier on Saturday, with the first run of the women’s GS kicking off at 10:00 CET. Shiffrin will then skip the traditional Slalom season openers in Levi and Gurgl - races she has won a combined 11 times - heading back to North America instead to focus on more GS in Killington and Tremblant, and then the speed events kicking off in Beaver Creek. Add on the fact that the season will open without Gut-Behrami, Sofia Goggia (ITA/Atomic), Federica Brignone (ITA/Rossignol) and Lindsey Vonn (USA/Head) – a quartet that boasts 198 World Cup wins between them – and it is no wonder intrigue levels are at their maximum. While Gut-Behrami has called time on her remarkable career, Goggia is hoping to have recovered from a pair of viral infections in time to start her defence of the Super G Globe in Beaver Creek, USA 11-13 December. Brignone will likely join her compatriot to train in North America but is unlikely to be ready to race. The 36-year-old had a further operation in August to remove a metal plate and screws from her leg and has barely put on skis since securing her stunning Olympic double. Vonn has been named in the wider USA ski team, but no date has been put on a possible comeback. A fifth icon, Petra Vlhova (SVK/Rossignol) is back however, ready to put smiles on faces. The 2022 Olympic Slalom champion will race in Sölden for the first time in three years after a challenging time blighted by injury. Three of those hoping to etch their name on the Overall Globe for the first time, Aicher, Camille Rast (SUI/Head) and Alice Robinson (NZL/Head) will be looking to jump ahead from the Sölden gun. If it is the German who continues her improvement in the GS – she landed her first two top-10s in the discipline in 2026 – then the others better watch out. Three wins in the Super G and two in the Downhill, plus five Slalom podiums, all in the past 18 months, surely places Aicher as the favourite to go one better than last season and succeed Shiffrin as the Big Globe champion. Rast may disagree. The only person other than Shiffrin to win a World Cup Slalom last season is primed to take full advantage of the American’s absence. The huge strides Rast took in the GS last season – a first win and top six finishes in eight out of 10 races – could be crucial too. A World Championships in her hometown of Crans-Montana also makes the Swiss star a favourite to defend her Slalom gold. Two years after becoming New Zealand’s first ever World Championship medal winner with silver in the GS, Robinson will hoping to go one better on Swiss snow. And, like her rivals, Robinson is now a real threat in more than one discipline. The GS wunderkid won last season’s SG opener in St Moritz, before following up with two second places in her next four races. While those three seem in prime position to step up, Laura Pirovano’s (ITA/Head) shock emergence showed nothing is predictable in ski racing. In early February the Italian had never been on a World Cup podium before, six weeks later she was Downhill champion, having won twice in two days in Val di Fassa and then, with everything on the line, producing one of the skis of the season at the World Cup Finals. Can she produce more of the same? Will reigning Olympic and world Downhill gold medallist Breezy Johnson (USA/Atomic) win a World Cup race? Can Julia Scheib (AUT/Rossignol) keep the Austrian smiles – and beer – flowing in Sölden with another season-setting GS victory? Talking of calendars, there are some riveting new stops to check out on the Audi World Cup tour this season, as well as returns to some favourite locations. The Austrian Alps are always the place to be during holiday season, but Dachstein West / Gosau may take that to new levels 28-29 December, with a women’s GS and Slalom ready to wow the crowds. That is not it for the Austrians, with Flachau getting a new year GS night race on 4 January, to go with the iconic starry-skied Slalom a night later. In a similar vein, the men will go in a new night Slalom in Alta Badia, alongside the popular GS. Elsewhere, Cortina and Lenzerheide are back on the women’s circuit, while the men’s tech skiers will go in Are, Sweden for the first time. Pinheiro Braathen will be among those looking to celebrate in Are. Although fascinatingly, the Brazilian will not only be seen on the short skis this winter. Months after beating Marco Odermatt (SUI/Stöckli) to both the Olympic and World Cup GS titles, Pinheiro Braathen is targeting “two missing pieces”. The first is taking the Big Globe from the Swiss man’s grasp. To do that Pinheiro Braathen knows he needs to start scoring points in a third discipline, the Super G. It will not be easy. Pinheiro Braathen has only ever started three World Cup Super G races. But having already landed Brazil a first ever Olympic medal and World Cup gong – and targeting the nation a first World Championship gold in February next year – the 26-year-old is used to defying expectation. The challenges to Odermatt’s reign will come thick and fast. Loic Meillard (SUI/Rossignol) is one of the men’s form skiers. Current Olympic and world Slalom champion, Meillard has finished second twice and third once in the past three GS Globe races. If he can start the season a little hotter – last time out it took until mid-December before he secured a first podium – the Rossignol man will challenge. Like his compatriot, Franjo von Allmen (SUI/Head) will head to Crans-Montana to defend World Championship gold. The young speedster has already shown he can do it on the biggest stages of all – three Olympic and two World titles – can he now do it week-in-week-out? Not that Odermatt will be quaking in his ski boots just yet. So dominant has the Stöckli skier been for so long that it is easy to overlook just how good he was last season. A fifth successive Overall crown, alongside the Downhill and Super G Globes and a second in the GS is seriously impressive. In fact, Odermatt has won 16 of 20 Globes he has competed for in the past five seasons. Although, a return of one gold (2025 Super G World Championships) and two silvers from his past two major championships, may mean Odi will prioritise Crans-Montana as the place to once again assert his authority. A longed-for win down the Streif in the Hahnenkamm Downhill on 23 January will also surely be circled in the diary. Unlike the women’s side, there is a fairly settled feeling to the men’s line-ups. Icons Dominik Paris (ITA/Nordica) – fresh from securing an Olympic bronze down his slope in Bormio – and Henrik Kristoffersen (NOR/Head) are back. Both will chase yet more glory. As will Clement Noël (FRA/Dynastar). The 2022 Olympic Slalom champion found a level of consistency last season (nine top 10s in 11 races) that if matched with even a proportion of the wins from previous seasons will mean a first Globe is in sight. Not that reigning Slalom World Cup champ Atle Lie McGrath (NOR/Head) will give his gong up easily. In the sad absence of Aleksander Aamodt Kilde (NOR/Atomic) who ruptured his Achilles tendon during pre-season in Chile, Italy’s new sensation Giovanni Franzoni (Rossignol) will join those looking to loosen Odermatt’s grip on the speed races. Excitingly, he will be joined by Marco Schwarz (AUT/Atomic). While not quite at Shiffrin’s level, the great Austrian all-rounder has surprised the Slalom world by deciding to hang up his short skis. Globe winner in 2021, Schwarz will pour all his energy into the Downhill, the Super G and the GS – starting in Sölden.

title: Navigating a System of AI Bottlenecks - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. The pace of AI transformation is often framed around the pace of model development, but the physical systems that are needed to responsibly scale that progress continue to operate across fundamentally different timelines. Power and data center supply chains remain critical bottlenecks1 for deployment and adoption, and the complex ecosystem of constraints has expanded to include transmission infrastructure, interconnection queues, permitting, equipment availability, community engagement, water considerations, and skilled labor, creating additional challenges for build-out. Goldman Sachs Research now expects global data center power demand to increase by 170% between 2025 and 2030, with more than 60% of that growth coming from within the United States. 2 But a constrained global supply chain may serve as a moderating force, with implications for the overall pace of AI growth and requisite capital fueling it. “Power is probably the forever bottleneck,” says Jason Tofsky, global head of Digital Infrastructure Investment Banking. “There are a lot of other bottlenecks that exist, and to get any one of these projects right, you have to get dozens of things right over a six-month to two-year time frame, including financing.” AI development continues to demand enormous amounts of compute, which, in turn, depends on a complex chain of physical infrastructure decisions. Baseline aggregate AI CapEx estimates hover around $7.6tn of capital between 2026 and 2031 across compute, data centers, and power. 3 Goldman Sachs Research is projecting $420bn of global hyperscaler debt issuance in 2027, representing a more than 60% increase from their FY2026 estimate. Notably, hyperscalers represent only 40% of the AI ecosystem credit raises. 4 A grid-connected data center requires approval from regulatory authorities, while a behind-the-meter project may avoid some grid constraints but can face air-permitting requirements and longer environmental reviews. At the local level, traffic, noise, emissions, water use, and the scale of construction concerns can meaningfully affect project timelines. Building a gigawatt-scale campus in a smaller community can reshape local roads and public-service demands almost overnight. The projects that move most effectively will likely address these considerations early through credible community-benefit commitments and transparent plans for environmental impact. The power system itself is also facing a growing set of constraints. The US interconnection queue has swelled to roughly 2,600 GW of generation and storage projects, more than double the installed capacity of the existing grid,5 although this figure includes projects at varying stages of maturity and potential overlap, says Tyler Miller, global co-head of Power, Utilities, and Infrastructure Investment Banking. The median time from interconnection application to commercial operation is now roughly five years, with some projects taking longer. The timeline challenge is not only the size of the interconnection queue, but also the pace at which the physical grid is expanding. US construction of new high-voltage transmission lines fell from an average of 1,700 miles annually between 2010 and 2014 to just 350 miles annually from 2020 to 2023, 5 according to Goldman Sachs Research. Transmission constraints are compounded by permitting and equipment shortages. Miller highlights that environmental reviews can take three to four years, while the lead times for high-voltage substations and generation step-up transformers have stretched to roughly three to five years. Local opposition adds another layer of complexity. Since January 2026, 86 projects have been canceled or extensively delayed, with 76 directly linked to local opposition. The concerns vary by market, ranging from water and emissions to noise, traffic, and potential pressure on residential electricity bills. The result is a growing interest in hybrid and behind-the-meter solutions. Repositioning Utilities for an Era of Higher Growth and Even Greater Capital For utilities, the implications of ongoing changes are profound. What was long viewed as a relatively low-growth, defensive sector is being repositioned as a capital-intensive engine of digital and real economies. Utility capital plans are increasing and expected to reach an aggregate $1.3tn between 2026 and 2030. 5 Capturing this opportunity requires a new playbook. Utilities and their large-load customers are increasingly considering structures in which hyperscalers contribute directly to the cost of generation, transmission, and substation infrastructure required to serve their facilities. The objective is much broader than just allocating costs; it is to ensure that new digital infrastructure strengthens the larger power system and delivers tangible benefits to local economies. The central principle is straightforward: “Growth enables growth,” Miller says. The demand for innovative financing across digital infrastructure and power has only grown more acute, as capital solutions must coordinate across land, development, power infrastructure, equipment, construction, and long-term operations. This new playing field calls for more flexible partnerships among utilities, hyperscalers, infrastructure investors, private-credit providers, insurers, and other long-duration pools of capital. As the bottlenecks evolve, capital solutions must do the same. This capital formation feeds a self-reinforcing cycle: More capacity enables faster model development and broader deployment, which, in turn, drives more demand. At the same time, model providers, hyperscalers, and chip companies are increasingly moving beyond their original layers in the AI stack. The infrastructure build-out also requires people—and in some markets, competing projects are bidding up wages to attract the same finite pool of workers. Labor shortages can disrupt even well-capitalized projects that have already secured land, power, and equipment. While finite labor may constrain the pace of deployment, the build-out is also creating well-paying, skilled blue-collar jobs across the country, broadening the economic benefits of AI beyond the technology sector. As a result, the AI infrastructure race has become a race to develop the workforce needed to build and operate this new industrial base. If power remains the binding constraint, AI growth will move at the speed of power delivery. Model capabilities advance in months; scaling generation, transmission, and equipment could take years. A likely result is a longer, less linear build-out, with capacity arriving in steps as more generation comes online. Longer timelines delay returns, increase risk, and widen the gap between projects with secured power and those still waiting. The same constraint imposes discipline: A more measured build-out allows demand to absorb investment over time, reducing the risk of stranded capital. This scenario introduces several important considerations: How much of this timing is already reflected in growth expectations? For markets that can add generation and grid capacity more quickly—for example, China—competitive advantages could emerge. The AI build-out continues to be as much a coordination challenge as a technological one. Significant advantages lie in addressing constraints together and early: engaging communities before seeking approvals, securing power and equipment ahead of need, developing the workforce, and structuring capital so that new demand funds the capacity it requires. 1 Powering the AI Era, Goldman Sachs Investment Banking (2025) 2 Masanet et al. (2020), EIA, EMBER, IEA, Cisco, Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research 3 Harnessing AI for the Real Economy, Goldman Sachs Investment Banking (2026) 4 Source: Dealogic (ION Analytics), Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research. As of September 15, 2026. Excludes data center financings issued by special purpose vehicles. Hyperscalers include Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle.
